title: Recap
lines: a1
In Episode 5, three frameworks agreed: comfort co-ords are Aalayam's best bet, sarees should stay a focused Kerala line, and the business needs evidence before it scales.
a2
That told us where to focus. Now the question is how to grow.

title: The growth challenge
lines: b1
Growth isn't simply launching more products or entering more markets. For a small brand, every new direction spreads the same team and budget thinner.
b2
And in the thousand to two thousand rupee band, competitors already sell similar co-ords, at twenty-six to sixty-nine percent off M R P.
b3
So the real question is: how can Aalayam grow, and stand out, without competing only on price?
b4
We used three tools. The Ansoff Matrix picks a growth direction. Blue Ocean Strategy looks for value competitors aren't offering. And the ERRC grid turns that into specific changes.
We used three tools. The Ansoff Matrix picks a growth direction. Blue Ocean Strategy looks for value competitors aren't offering. And the E R R C grid turns that into specific changes.

title: Ansoff Matrix
lines: c1
The Ansoff Matrix crosses products with markets, giving four growth directions. We scored thirteen ideas on attractiveness and feasibility.
c2

Market penetration: sell more of today's products to today's customers. Fit-transparent product pages and a WhatsApp review loop score high, because they're cheap and fix known doubts. But deeper discounts? Avoid. That's a price war Aalayam can't win.
c3

Market development: Malayali women in Bengaluru, Chennai and Mumbai are a good next step. NRI shipping is attractive but risky, because international exchanges are slow and costly. So that stays a waitlist.
c4
Product development: new products for today's customers. The top idea is a fit-confident comfort co-ord, where top and bottom come in separate sizes, with a Kerala design detail.
c5
Diversification, into kidswear, tailoring or home textiles, would spread a small team even thinner. Not now.
c6
So the primary direction is product development. Penetration ideas score as high, but any competitor can copy a size chart. They become the enablers, not the strategy.

title: Competitive landscape
lines: d1
Next, why fit? Look at how competitors actually compete.
d2
Mass brands and unbranded sellers compete on price, discounts and range. Libas alone lists about three hundred co-ords. And almost everyone sells a set in one size for top and bottom.
d3
Meanwhile, fit is the main complaint in reviews, and industry estimates put fashion returns at twenty to thirty percent, driven mostly by size and fit.
d4
Custom fit does exist, but mostly at premium prices, often with weeks of waiting and no returns.

title: Blue Ocean opportunities
lines: e1
Blue Ocean Strategy asks a different question: instead of beating rivals on the same factors, what value could Aalayam create that the market isn't offering?
e2

We developed three potential concepts. One: fit-confident comfort co-ords. Two: Kerala everyday, a regional design for daily wear, not just festivals. Three: winning women who skip online clothing and go to a tailor instead.
e3
None of these is a proven blue ocean yet. But the first has the strongest evidence, so we take it forward, with the Kerala detail as its design layer.

title: Strategy canvas
lines: f1
Here's the strategy canvas. Each line is a value curve across eight factors customers weigh. The scores are our research-based estimates, not customer ratings.
f2
Unbranded sellers and mass brands follow the same shape: high on discounts and range, low on fit information and flexibility.
f3
Premium brands solve fit, but at two to three times the price.
f4
Aalayam's proposed curve breaks away. Fewer discounts, a narrower range, and much more fit information, fit flexibility and personal help, at a mid price. These are targets, not current performance.

title: ERRC grid
lines: g1
The ERRC grid makes that concrete.
The E R R C grid makes that concrete.
g2
Eliminate: the inflated M R P with constant discounts, and the rule that a set comes in one size.
g3
Reduce: the range, to six to eight core silhouettes, and dependence on marketplaces.
g4
Raise: fit information, with garment measurements, model size, fit notes and daylight photos. Make one size exchange free. And strengthen the Kerala identity.
g5
Create: split sizing with an adjustable waist and two lengths, and a WhatsApp fit check that remembers each customer's sizes.
g6
The value proposition shifts from comfortable, stylish and accessible, which everyone claims, to comfort co-ords that fit the first time.

title: Strategic synthesis
lines: h1
Put together: Ansoff points to product development. Blue Ocean points to fit confidence at a mid price. And ERRC defines the offer.
h2
This builds on Episode 5. Same hero category, same Kerala signature. What's new is that fit moves from a supporting action to the core of the positioning.
h3
The target customer: women aged twenty-four to thirty-eight, in Kerala and in Indian metros, buying everyday co-ords online, who've struggled with fit.
h4

It needs separate top and bottom stock, measured garments, and time on WhatsApp. The risks: demand for split sizing may be small, inventory can fall out of balance, and exchanges cost money. So we test first.

title: 90-day roadmap
lines: j1
Days one to thirty: validate. Interview fifteen to twenty customers, survey how often top and bottom sizes differ, audit five competitors, and record a baseline from Shopify.
j2
Days thirty-one to sixty: experiment. Launch a six-piece fit-confident capsule on pre-order, with fit-transparent pages, a WhatsApp fit check and one honest price.
j3
Days sixty-one to ninety: decide. Compare conversion, size-related returns and exchange costs with the baseline. Then scale, iterate or stop. The next milestone is Malayali women in the metros.
j4
No targets are invented here. Every goal is set against Aalayam's own baseline.

title: Closing
lines: k1
Aalayam doesn't need to be the cheapest, or the biggest. It can grow by solving the problem customers complain about most, and making fit its promise.
k2
That's Episode 6 of the Aalayam business research series.
